items.desc:
The Adventurer is a high-poly sculpt of a stylized young explorer: messy red hair, a cheerful face, a knit sweater, cargo pants and sneakers, and a big hiking backpack carrying a bedroll and a water bottle. The look is clean and appealing, close to modern animated-film style.

The shapes stay simple and readable while each material keeps its own feel: soft knit folds in the sweater, heavier canvas in the pants and pack, and leather straps and buckles on the backpack. The backpack is sculpted as its own piece, so it can be swapped or removed in game. This is the high-poly stage, ready for retopology, baking and texturing to whatever budget a project needs.

Need stylized heroes with a friendly, film-quality look? We can match this look, or take it wherever your project needs to go.

Monster Lizard is a realistic enemy creature: a hulking, low-slung reptile with a toothy grin, a ridge of dark spines down its back, mottled armored hide and a long, heavy tail. It's built to be the thing that charges out of the dark in an action or survival game.

The sculpt is all about weight and anatomy: thick shoulders and forearms, a body that sags between the legs, and scales and plates that change size across the body so the hide never looks tiled. It fits in about 34K tris and a single 4K texture set, shown in Unreal Engine, with clean topology ready for a quadruped rig.

items.desc:
We made CHR Skins to show what a cosmetics pipeline looks like when it's built for volume. Every outfit is a set of swappable pieces (top, layer, jeans, shoes) on one shared base body, so new skins come from recombining and retexturing, not rebuilding.

Five base sets (hoodie, shirt, leather jacket, denim jacket and sleeveless denim vest) become 15 distinct looks through color, wash and wear passes. Swap the tops, bottoms and shoes between them and you get hundreds of casual outfits, with fabric that reads as real fleece, cotton and denim at gameplay distance. Topology stays consistent across pieces, so skin weights carry over and everything mixes and matches without clipping.

Need a steady stream of skins for a multiplayer, live-service or streetwear-style game? We'll build yours to your style, budget and platform.

items.desc:
Female Hair is the groom we built for SWAT V3: a messy high bun with loose strands falling around the face and flyaways at the hairline and nape. Messy buns are hard in real time, because the volume has to look full without turning into a solid shape.

The hair is built from layered alpha cards on a single 4K texture set, at 60K tris. Base layers give the volume, mid layers the strand clumps, and fine cards on top add flyaways and break up the silhouette, so it reads as hair from every angle, even straight down on top of the head. The card layout is set up for hair shaders, wind and physics.

Need hair that holds up on a hero character? We'll build yours to your style, budget and platform.

Male Hair Variations is one short men's haircut built as a full hair-loss progression: a full head of hair at the first stage, thinning step by step through a receding hairline and crown to a balding pattern. It's made for character customization and aging systems, where one style has to work at every age.

Each stage is its own alpha-card groom on a shared 4K texture set, and the tri count drops as the hair thins, from 45K at the first stage to 25K at the last, so the lighter versions cost less in game. The hairline and crown stay natural at every stage, without the hard edges you get when cards are simply deleted.

items.desc:
Sir Galahad is our take on the lead knight from The Order: 1886, built from scratch to match a AAA cinematic look. The goal was simple: could our version hold up in the same kind of close-up shots as the original?

The uniform does most of the talking: a wool coat with gold braiding, a leather belt rig with holster and dagger, an embroidered cape emblem, and engraved steel bracers and greaves, each with its own wear and edge breakup. The face and beard are sculpted for close-ups, and the coat and cape are built as clean quad meshes, ready for rigging and cloth sim.

Adam is a five-stage progression character: one stylized boy who grows from a schoolkid into a fully armored warrior. Each stage adds gear on top of the last, so the player sees the journey on the model itself.

Stage 1 is the base schoolboy, stage 2 adds a rebel's mask, vest and pouches, stage 3 a bow and quiver, stage 4 a sword and light armor, and stage 5 the full knight set with crested helmet, cape and shield. Everything sits on one base body and skeleton, so gear attaches and swaps cleanly. The budget stays low and texturing starts from a single 2K map, so the full set runs on mobile and Switch as well as PC.

Explorer's Book (first made as our Proposal Book) came out of a 12-week masterclass our team took on the game prop pipeline. It's an explorer's kit packed onto one book: a green embossed leather journal strapped shut, a rolled bamboo mat, a spyglass, a quill and pencil, wax-sealed letters, coins, dice and loose sketch pages.

The challenge was making a pile of small objects read as one prop. Leather, paper, bamboo, brass and glass each get their own wear, and the loose pages and straps are arranged so the silhouette works from any angle. It's built to be seen up close, on a desk, in an inspect view or in a story moment.

Fire Drum is a hand-pumped coal furnace: a dented red drum stove full of glowing coals, a wooden bellows feeding air through a wrapped cloth hose, and a pan of coal beside a stack of metal plates. It's the sort of working prop that makes a blacksmith's corner, a street vendor or a survival camp feel lived in.

Every surface shows how it's been used: chipped paint and rust on the drum, scorch marks around the air holes, soot on the plates, and frayed, dusty fabric on the hose. It sits at 14K tris with three 2K texture sets (drum, coals and bellows), and the coals are set up for emissive glow and particles in engine.

The sculpt sets the big forms first, then the wrinkles, pores and scar tissue that sell his age. Head Study is a likeness sculpt of actor Benedict Wong, done in ZBrush as a pure anatomy and likeness exercise. Likeness work leaves nowhere to hide: if the proportions, or the fat and muscle under the skin, are off even slightly, the face stops looking like the person.

The focus is on the forms under the skin: the fullness of the cheeks and jowls, the weight around the eyes and mouth, the folds of the neck, and the pores and fine wrinkles on top. It's the kind of high-poly head a game team bakes from for a hero character or a digital double.
